%% The abstract is a short summary of the work to be presented in the
%% article.
\begin{abstract}
The Raspberry Pi is a miniature general-purpose computer that has found widespread usage in a variety of settings. It also suffers
from an issue that is all too common with IoT devices: a vulnerable framework that makes it easy for malevolent actors to attack
the device and systems that it supports. In our experiment, we set out to examine the Raspberry Pi 3's vulnerabilities by carrying out 
SSH Server Hardening on the Pi, followed by executing the Log4Shell attack on an Apache server using Log4j, with the server being hosted 
on the Pi 3. We encountered several issues, such as downgrading Java to Java 8 and setting up an LDAP server to carry out the Log4Shell 
attack, but we were ultimately successful in executing the attack. While the Log4Shell vulnerability was patched soon after its discovery, our 
experiment showcases how devastating it was, something exacerbated by the sheer number of services using Log4j.

\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

%Background
Raspberry Pi has become one of the foremost names for their wide array of miniature general-purpose computers. These
devices are used ubiquitously across industrial, commercial, and home scales for automation, IoT, and general purpose computing.
Their prevalence and reliability also makes them a popular target for cyberattacks. The exploitation of a Raspberry Pi could
lead to the downfall of an entire cyber-physical system, especially if not configured properly. 

%Current Problems
Our goal was to explore the security considerations of the Raspberry Pi when deploying the device for a particular task: hosting a web
server. We set up an Apache web server on the Pi alongside a Maven middleend and Springboot backend. Initially, we wanted to
test the Pi against several different types of attacks (such as the ones mentioned in section \ref{sec:relatedWork}), but due to time
constraints, we decided to focus on one notorious vulnerability: Log4Shell. This involved setting up an LDAP server that acted
as the attacker's server, targeting the Pi's Apache server.


%Current Solutions -> i.e. what has already been done, but nothing we've done is novel so be sure not to frame our work as somehow improving on current solutions 
In this paper, we offer the following contributions:
%Contributions
% Server Hardening
% Log4Shell Replication
% Examination of the Security Flaws that allowed log4shell to occur
\begin{itemize}
  \item An examination of IoT device security through SSH Server Hardening on Raspberry Pi 3
  \item A replication and partial toolchain for exploitation of the Log4Shell vulnerability on an Apache2 web server
  \item An analysis of the vulnerabilities present in Log4j enabling our exploit chain
\end{itemize}


\section{Background}
The Raspberry Pi 3 Model B that we used is an embedded or single board computer with the Raspbian operating 
system installed. As an IoT device, it is capable of a wide array of actions (such as hosting
a web server) but it is also subject to many flaws and vulnerabilities that make it easy for 
malevolent actors to carry out a suite of attacks against it. For example, the default username
and password of a user on the Raspbian operating system is "pi" and "raspberry", respectively. 
Failing to change these credentials makes it quite simple for an attack to gain access to one's device
\cite{ARREAGA2023223}. Various attacks have been demonstrated against the device to highlight its 
fragile security framework, including Man-in-the-Middle (MITM), backdoor, and DoS attacks \cite{ARREAGA2023223}. 
We will delve further into these experiments in section \ref{sec:relatedWork}.

For this particular experiment that we ran, we focused on an attack that exploited
a vulnerability with Log4j. Log4j is a library that is used to create log messages that
track all sorts of events \cite{Holla}. It enjoys widespread usage across many different
applications, including web frameworks and even the hit video game \textit{Minecraft}
\cite{Chierici}. Due to the sheer amount of products and services that were using Log4j,
mass panic and alarm ensued when a vulnerability was discovered within it in December
2021, with this vulnerability being called Log4Shell. The Log4Shell exploit allowed attackers 
to carry out malicious code on targeted servers \cite{Holla}.

\begin{figure}[h]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.50\textwidth]{LDAPAttack}
    \caption{Layout of the LDAP Attack on Log4j \cite{Holla}.}
    \label{fig:ldapAttack}
\end{figure}

Figure \ref{fig:ldapAttack} summarizes the attack that we conducted but we will go over the details
here. Versions of Log4j with the Log4Shell incorrectly handle Java Naming and Directory Interface (JNDI)
requests. JNDI requests are used as lookups for particular resources; these JNDI requests use URLs
that lead to a different server (such as an LDAP or DNS server) \cite{INCIBE}. Malevolent actors could 
thus set up their own server and then send a log message to a victim application server that uses a version 
of Log4j with the Log4Shell exploit. The log message sent by the attacker is a JNDI lookup that contains a URL
that directs the user to their server. Upon receiving this message, the application server has Log4j go 
through it. Upon performing the JNDI lookup, code from the attacker's own server is executed on the
victim server, leading to potentially catastrophic results \cite{Holla}. Depending on the attacker's motive,
the malicious code could cause anything from data leaks to server shutdowns.



\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:relatedWork}
While we did not do a full literature review of the material, the main article that inspired this investigation of 
ours was a set of experiments run by researchers Arreaga et al., in which they tested three different types 
of attacks (MITM, backdoor, and DoS) on a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B device with the Raspbian operating 
system. The researchers also performed the same suite of attacks on a VM that had the Windows 10 OS 
installed in order to compare the times for the attacks to be carried out. The goal of their research, like ours, 
was to highlight the major security flaws present in IoT devices, which are becoming more and more widely 
used. The authors note that with billions of IoT devices estimated to be in use by 2025, the opportunities for 
attackers to carry out devastating attacks against these devices (and thus the frameworks and systems they 
support) will only grow \cite{ARREAGA2023223}.

As for the results, the researchers were able to successfully execute all three attacks on both machines.
The total time to carry out the MITM and DoS attacks (which includes the setup and execution times) was
the same across both devices, but it was quicker to carry out the backdoor attack against the Raspberry Pi
than the Windows 10 VM. The authors note that the Raspberry Pi lacks "built-in virus and intrusion detection 
software," software which the Windows 10 VM had, making it relatively easier to attack the Pi \cite{ARREAGA2023223}. Their findings
highlight the treatment of security as a bonus feature or add-on with IoT devices, which (when considering the
widespread usage of these devices) can lead to disastrous consequences the likes of which no one has seen
before (including data breaches, service disruptions and shutdowns, and more). The authors recommend
some potential fixes to protect the Pi from these attacks, such as using a secure HTTPS protocol and limiting
traffic from a host, but they also warn about other potential attacks (such as DNS cache poisoning and
TCP sequence attacks) \cite{ARREAGA2023223}.



\section{Ethical Statement}

All attacks were performed only using machines owned and operated by the authors. The devices were connected to
CalPoly's eduroam network. However, no regular network traffic was disrupted, harmed, or observed during any activities performed
over the course of this study. Additionally, the authors worked primarily to replicate known strategies for exploitation of a downpatched
Log4j, all of which have been fixed in any modern version of Java and the Log4j package from the last 5 years. 

\section{System Design}

This section offers description and details about our Raspberry Pi server configuration, attacker resources, and 
our specific exploit chain. Code for the main components of our setup and attack can be found in our archive, submitted
in tandem with this report. 

\subsection{SSH Hardening}

Prior to launching the Log4Shell attack, we took steps to close off easier avenues for attack on the Raspberry Pi, a
process commonly known as "server hardening". These steps are detailed from the tutorials followed, provided here \cite{sshKeys} and
here \cite{sshHardening}. However, we also offer brief description of the motivation behind these steps.

First and foremost, all SSH public keys of the authors were added to the authorized key list of the Pi. This allowed usage
to disable SSH Authentication via any means besides public key authentication. This is desirable due to the favorable 
security benefits offered by public key cryptography which are not present in the default, password-based login. Namely,
passwords are often crackable when configured lazily, phished from users, or present within known leaked password corpora. 
Our Raspberry Pi user credentials were no different, using the default username/password for a single sudo-enabled user.

The SSH port for the Raspberry Pi was also changed to 4707, away from the default of 22. This was done to prevent  
port scanner attacks, wherein common and default network ports on a machine are targeted by attackers for potential weakpoints.
Login as root was entirely disabled, instead opting to do all administrative tasks from our sudo-enabled user account. 
Full control when acting as the root user itself can be risky, and for our purposes it was never a necessary exposure.
Other server hardening tricks such as disabling outdated/insecure SSH protocols, firewalling, IP-banning, and whitelisting,
all of which are suggested in \cite{sshHardening}, were examined but not implemented on our server for the sake of time.

\subsection{Raspberry Pi Apache Server}

Our system was designed with three distinct pieces: an Apache server running the frontend static website, 
a Maven project for package imports and project structure, and a Spring Boot backend that 
connected the webpage inputs to the logging channel.

Our main motivation for using Apache to host a web page was that the page would be on a static IP address that 
we could access from outside of the Raspberry Pi. Thus, our Apache server is very generic. We followed a tutorial to set it up \cite{Islam}, 
and the only deviations were editing the HTML to give us input boxes for username and password, and adding a CSS 
file to make the page look more complete. 

We chose to create a Maven project in order to use Log4j because the recommended way to use Log4j was through a package manager 
like Maven or Gradle, and we had more prior experience with Maven. We followed the Maven in 5 Minutes tutorial \cite{Maven} in order to 
set up the project, and then began editing the POM file to add the necessary dependencies for logging and our backend. 
We also made edits to App.java, the main Java file created by the Maven project initialization, in order to test initial 
logging and set up a Spring Boot application.

In our App.java, we initialized Spring Boot with the @SpringBootApplication decorator and also ran the Spring application in main. 
The backend uses a REST API to communicate with our web page, fielding inputs into the Log4j logging system and printing them to standard out. 
One of the design choices that we made in order for the Log4Shell attack to work was we did not sanitize our inputs. This meant that whatever
inputs were sent through the frontend web page were directly ported through the backend to Log4j. Although this is now thought of as bad practice,
this was one of the necessary steps for the exploit to work.

\subsection{Attacker Servers}

In our simulation, our attacker hosted a Lightweight Directory Access Protocol server to serve malicious responses to
vulnerable JNDI requests from Log4j. OpenLDAP was installed via the apt repository on our attacker's Debian 12 laptop.
A domain name "exampleproject.com" was assigned as a reference for the attacker's machine IP address.    
A java.ldif was added to the LDAP schema to allow lookups to javaObject, javaCodebase, javaClassName, javaFactory, and javaNamingReference.
This schema was necessary for JNDI to be able to receive exploit payloads when querying the LDAP server.

The attacker also hosted an HTTP server on port 8000 via Python 3.12's http.server module. This served GET requests directly
from the attacker's file hierarchy to any node on the same network. This server is resolves the request from the 
LDAP schema to deliver the payload back to the original JNDI request. There may have been a way to host the exploit.jar file
directly within the LDAP server instead of resolving the request through a local HTTP server, akin to the depiction in \ref{fig:ldapAttack}, 
but this method worked ammicably as well. 

\subsection{Attack Execution}

Log4j had two critical vulnerabilities leading to the Remote Code Execution (RCE). The first is execution of unsantized user input
for the purposes of logging. On the Apache server's webpage, there was a user name and password field, that when submitted to
would take the user to a new page greeting them by name, and update the logs to include the new login attempt. However, any 
string included in the username field would be executed as though included in the Log4j format string. This meant that 
\texttt{\$\{text\}} strings would be evaluated. This could be used for banal things, such as \texttt{\$\{jvm:version\}} would 
add the current Java version within the logged entry. However, JNDI lookups were also available within these strings, allowing the 
attacker to force the server to resolve a resource from arbitrary destinations. This lack of santization was a default 
in Log4j 2.14.1.

The second vulnerability was another dangerous default prior to the release of Log4Shell. The system property
\texttt{com.sun.jndi.ldap.
object.trustURLCodebase} was set to \texttt{true}. In our Apache server, we had to set this 
condition manually in order to make the attack possible, despite running versions of Java and Log4j older than the patch
of the Log4Shell vulnerabilities. We are not sure why this is, but are still confident that at some point in the past,
this was a default. The danger of this option is allowing all LDAP servers requested for JNDI lookup to have trusted code 
automatically. By trusting the code automatically, it is executed immediately upon resource retrieval. This component, combined 
with the first vulnerability, completes an exploit chain that allows any attacker to set up an LDAP server and point
an Apache server to execute an arbitrary payload.   

The attack payload we chose was a Java class which implemented the ObjectFactory interface, aptly named ExploitFactory. Upon retrieval by the JNDI query, the
ExploitFactory's getObjectInstance method performs two actions. First, using a PrintWriter, it writes a file to the home directory of the pi user
with the message "you got pwned!" It then starts a ProcessBuilder executing /bin/bash taking and sending all inputs over TCP to port 31415 on
the attacker's IP address. This is more commonly known as a reverse shell, as it allows the attacker, when listening on their chosen port,
to interact with a bash shell on the Raspberry Pi's directory hierarchy despite not having the authentication or public keys registered on the device. 
We note that no behaviors were performed that required root access from the Raspberry Pi. However, the reverse shell is certainly
a powerful enough technique to perform reconnaissance and privilege escalation, allowing the attacker to do essentially whatever they wish. 


\section{Lessons Learned}

We learned that Log4j can be potentially quite dangerous, as we were able to write a reverse shell with not a ton of setup. It seems
like the best defenses are just to be up to date on software. The specific vulnerability we exploited was removed starting in Log4j version
2.17, but there were various security patches along the way as well. Additionally, having proper input hygiene would also have prevented
the attack, or at least made it much more difficult. 

It was nearly impossible to find resources about how to exploit Log4j, as it is a CVE 10 vulnerability. It was quite easy to
learn about what the attack was, however, so most of our time was spent reverse-engineering the attack from the resources available to us.
There were a handful of repositories online that claimed to test for and/or exploit Log4j, but we didn't want to run them locally and
it was difficult to run them on a more protected tool such as Google Colab, as many of them were OS dependent or required Docker.

One major pain of this project was the arduous adventure to downgrade Java. The initial version of Java that was on
the Pi was openJDK 25, but we wanted to downgrade it to Java 8 since we believed that would have made the attack
easier to carry out. However, this turned out to be much more of a struggle than we had anticipated. We tried various
methods, such as using additional plugins from Maven that we learned about from Stack Overflow posts and even
restarting Maven on the Pi. Eventually, we learned from another Stack Overflow post that we had to install a Debian
mirror (since we were using Raspbian on the Pi), which finally allowed us to downgrade to Java 8. It is difficult for us
to pinpoint what the takeaway here exactly is. We knew we wanted a downgraded version of Java and we tried out
several different strategies that seemed reasonable to us, only for those to fail. But at least now we know for next
time what the ultimate solution is.

\section{Conclusion}

This project explored the intersection of IoT and Web Security through an exploit-focused lens of the Log4Shell attack.
The Raspberry Pi 3 served as an isolated but fully operational testbed for server hosting. Our SSH server hardening
demonstrated considerations of access control for IoT devices, while the Apache server hosting and subsequent exploit
encompassed both desirebale user function for the Raspberry Pi as a device (by hosting a webpage on the local network) 
and the consequences of web vulnerabilities which enable full-system Remote Code Execution. The replication of the Log4Shell
attack showed that a vulnerability on one component of our Raspberry Pi server lead to the compromise of the entire device 
through a reverse shell.
